Three mandatory skill sets: interpersonal, technical, conceptual
Three defining features of formal organizations: purpose, specialized labor, hierarchical authority
Organizational hierarchy: top executives, middle managers, frontline staff
Manager types: general, public/non-profit, line, functional
Manager levels: top, middle, frontline, project lead
Three formal managerial role categories: informational, interpersonal, decisional
10 specific managerial duties: monitor, disseminator, spokesperson, figurehead, leader, liaison, entrepreneur, conflict mediator, resource allocator, negotiator

title: BOH4M Exit Card Learning Package
problemAnchor: 本节课的核心概念（Managers vs Leaders、Four Management Functions）之间有什么联系？学生在理解上最容易卡在哪里？

abt.and: 你已经完成了本节课的学习。
abt.but: 但是不同概念之间的联系可能还没有建立起来，容易被零散记忆。
abt.therefore: 系统先诊断你卡在哪个知识节点，再用对应补救模块带你重新理解，最后用复测确认是否真正连起来。

objective: Managers are distinct from leaders; they support others' work and take formal responsibility for collective outputs.；The four core management functions are planning, organizing, leading, and controlling.；All managers need three skill sets: interpersonal (communication), technical (office software), and conceptual (big-picture problem-solving).

questions.stem: A classmate says: 'Managers and leaders are basically the same thing — both just tell people what to do.' Based on today’s lesson, which response best reflects what you learned?
questions.successCriteria: Student identifies that managers and leaders are distinct, with managers supporting others' work and taking formal responsibility for collective outputs.
questions.ossdExpectation: Assess the role of management within an organization.
questions.alignmentNote: Directly addresses the role and definition of management vs leadership.
questions.stemIntent: Check whether students can distinguish managers from leaders based on formal responsibility and support role.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may think managers and leaders are interchangeable terms, ignoring the formal responsibility and support aspects of management.

options.label: A
options.text: You're right — they are essentially the same; the words are just used in different contexts.
options.feedbackWrong: Not exactly. In the lesson we learned that managers and leaders are distinct. Managers support others' work and carry formal responsibility for team outputs.

options.label: B
options.text: Managers and leaders are different. Leaders focus on formal authority, while managers focus on vision.
options.feedbackWrong: That's reversed. Leaders often provide vision, while managers hold formal authority and responsibility for collective outputs.

options.label: C
options.text: Managers and leaders are distinct. Managers support others' work and take formal responsibility for collective outputs, whereas leaders may not have that formal role.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! You've captured the key distinction from the lesson.

options.label: D
options.text: Managers are always leaders, but not all leaders are managers.
options.feedbackWrong: This is not quite accurate. While some managers also lead, the lesson emphasized that the roles are distinct in terms of formal responsibility and support.

questions.stem: A manager at a tech company needs to identify potential growth opportunities and plan for the next quarter. Which managerial skill set is most critical for this task?
questions.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies conceptual skills as the primary skill for big-picture problem-solving and strategic planning.
questions.ossdExpectation: Assess the role of management within an organization.
questions.alignmentNote: Skill sets are part of understanding management roles.
questions.stemIntent: Check whether students can match the appropriate skill set (interpersonal, technical, conceptual) to a real-world managerial task.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may think technical skills are most important for planning, or that interpersonal skills dominate all tasks.

options.label: A
options.text: Interpersonal skills — because you need to communicate with the team to gather ideas.
options.feedbackWrong: Good to communicate, but the core of identifying opportunities and planning is big-picture thinking. That's conceptual skills.

options.label: B
options.text: Technical skills — because you need to use software to analyze data.
options.feedbackWrong: While technical skills may help, the higher-order task of envisioning growth and strategic planning relies on conceptual skills.

options.label: C
options.text: Conceptual skills — because this involves big-picture problem-solving and strategic direction.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Conceptual skills are about thinking broadly and strategically.

options.label: D
options.text: All three are equally critical for this task.
options.feedbackWrong: Although all skill sets are useful, conceptual skills are most directly needed for strategic planning and identifying opportunities.

questions.stem: During a weekly staff meeting, a manager listens to team updates, shares information from upper management, and decides to form a new task force to address a recurring problem. This manager is performing which categories of managerial roles?
questions.successCriteria: Student identifies that the manager is performing informational (monitor, disseminator) and decisional (entrepreneur) roles.
questions.ossdExpectation: Assess the role of management within an organization.
questions.alignmentNote: Managerial roles are part of the management role assessment.
questions.stemIntent: Check students' ability to categorize managerial behaviors into the three role categories (informational, interpersonal, decisional).
questions.commonMisconception: Students may confuse informational with interpersonal roles, or miss that decision-making is a distinct category.

options.label: A
options.text: Only informational roles, because the manager is listening and sharing information.
options.feedbackWrong: Listening and sharing are indeed informational, but forming a new task force is a decisional role. So both categories are used.

options.label: B
options.text: Interpersonal roles, because the manager is interacting with the team.
options.feedbackWrong: Interpersonal roles involve relationships, but here the main actions are information exchange and decision-making, which fall under informational and decisional.

options.label: C
options.text: Informational roles (monitor and disseminator) and decisional roles (entrepreneur – initiating a new project).
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Listening and sharing are informational; forming a task force to solve a problem is a decisional role.

options.label: D
options.text: All three categories: informational, interpersonal, and decisional.
options.feedbackWrong: While the meeting involves interaction, the interpersonal roles (like figurehead or liaison) are not explicitly demonstrated here beyond normal conversation. The primary roles are informational and decisional.

miniLesson.explain: Managers and leaders are distinct concepts. Managers support others' work and take formal responsibility for collective outputs. Leaders may inspire but do not necessarily have formal authority. The four core management functions are planning, organizing, leading, and controlling. All managers need three skill sets: interpersonal (communication), technical (office software), and conceptual (big-picture problem-solving).
miniLesson.example: In the lesson, a class poll unanimously considered Steve Jobs a strong manager, yet he was also a visionary leader. A manager like a project manager ensures deadlines are met and reports to executives, while a leader might inspire innovation without that formal accountability. The distinction is about formal responsibility.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Managers have the Mandate (formal responsibility); Leaders have the Vision (may lack formal role).

guidedPractice.prompt: True or False: According to the lesson, managers and leaders are basically the same thing because both guide people.
guidedPractice.answer: False. Managers are distinct from leaders; they support others' work and take formal responsibility for collective outputs.

guidedPractice.prompt: A person at a company is responsible for assigning tasks, tracking progress, and reporting results to upper management. Would you classify this person as a manager or a leader? Explain using lesson facts.
guidedPractice.answer: This person is a manager. The lesson states that managers support others' work and take formal responsibility for collective outputs, which matches assigning tasks and reporting results. Leaders may not have such formal accountability.

guidedPractice.prompt: Compare and contrast the roles of a manager and a leader, using at least one example from the lesson and one of the three managerial skill sets.
guidedPractice.answer: Managers take formal responsibility for collective outputs and support others' work, as seen in the example of Steve Jobs being considered a strong manager. Leaders may inspire but lack formal authority. For instance, a manager uses conceptual skills for big-picture planning, while a leader might rely on interpersonal skills to motivate. Both are important, but their roles differ in responsibility and authority.

reteachModules.trigger: Student fails to list or identify all four management functions, or selects an incorrect function as one of the four.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student may think management functions include tasks like staffing, directing, or budgeting, rather than the core four: planning, organizing, leading, and controlling.

miniLesson.explain: The four core management functions are planning, organizing, leading, and controlling. Planning involves setting goals and deciding how to achieve them. Organizing arranges resources and tasks. Leading motivates and directs people. Controlling monitors progress and makes corrections.
miniLesson.example: For a school fundraiser: planning sets the goal and strategy; organizing assigns roles and gathers supplies; leading inspires the team; controlling tracks donations and adjusts if needed.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember the acronym POLC: Planning, Organizing, Leading, Controlling.

guidedPractice.prompt: List the four core management functions.
A manager schedules team meetings, assigns tasks, and sets deadlines. Which management function is being performed?

A project manager creates a timeline (planning), forms sub-teams (organizing), motivates team members during delays (leading), and compares actual progress to the timeline (controlling). Which four functions are demonstrated?

options: A leader because they inspire their team
A manager because they take formal responsibility for collective outputs
Both a manager and a leader equally
Neither a manager nor a leader

questions.stem: Explain the distinction between managers and leaders as presented in the lesson. In your answer, reference at least one example from the lesson and describe why this distinction matters in an organization.
questions.rubric: Student must clearly state that managers have formal responsibility for collective outputs and support others' work, while leaders may inspire but do not necessarily hold formal authority. They should mention a lesson example (e.g., Steve Jobs poll, personal stories) and explain that the distinction clarifies roles and expectations within an organization's hierarchy.
